Content:
De Moivre's theorem provides a simple way to compute powers of complex numbers in polar form. It states that
[MATH: \left[ \cos (\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)},]

Content:
where [MATH: n] is an integer.

Content:
For example, let's use De Moivre's theorem to compute [MATH: \left[ \cos (3\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(3\theta) \right]^5.] We get

Content:
[MATH: [\cos (3θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (3θ)]^{5}|= \cos (5 ⋅ 3θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (5 ⋅ 3θ); = \cos (15θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (15θ).]

De Moivre's Theorem states that [MATH: \left[ \cos(\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)}.]

In our expression, we have [MATH: n=-2] and [MATH: \varphi=\theta.] Substituting in these values, we get [MATH: (1)/([\cos (θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (θ)]^{2})|= [\cos (θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (θ)]^{− 2}; = \cos (− 2θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (− 2θ).]

Finally, using the fact that [MATH: \cos(-\varphi) = \cos (\varphi)] and [MATH: \sin(-\varphi) = -\sin(\varphi)] for any input [MATH: \varphi,] we have [MATH: \cos(-2\theta) + \textrm{i}\sin(-2\theta) = \cos(2\theta) - \textrm{i}\sin{(2\theta)}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
De Moivre's theorem provides a simple way to compute powers of complex numbers in polar form. It states that
[MATH: \left[ \cos (\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)},]

Content:
where [MATH: n] is an integer.

Content:
For example, let's use De Moivre's theorem to compute [MATH: \left[ \cos (3\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(3\theta) \right]^5.] We get

Content:
[MATH: [\cos (3θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (3θ)]^{5}|= \cos (5 ⋅ 3θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (5 ⋅ 3θ); = \cos (15θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (15θ).]

---

Item 2 — Example: Applying De Moivre's Theorem

Example Prompt:
Simplify the expression [MATH: \left[ \cos \left( \dfrac{\theta}{10} \right) + \textrm{i}\sin \left( \dfrac{\theta}{10}\right) \right]^4.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
De Moivre's Theorem states that
[MATH: \left[ \cos(\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)}.]

In our expression, we have [MATH: n=4] and [MATH: \varphi=\dfrac{\theta}{10}.] Substituting in these values, we get
[MATH: [\cos ((θ)/(10)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((θ)/(10))]^{4}|= \cos (4 ⋅ (θ)/(10)) + \textrm{i}\sin (4 ⋅ (θ)/(10)); = \cos ((2θ)/(5)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((2θ)/(5)).]

---

Item 5 — Example: Applying De Moivre's Theorem to Fractions

Example Prompt:
Simplify the expression [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\left[ \cos (\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(\theta) \right]^2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, note that
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{\left[ \cos(\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(\theta) \right]^2} = \left[ \cos(\theta) +\textrm{i}\sin(\theta) \right]^{-2} .]

De Moivre's Theorem states that
[MATH: \left[ \cos(\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) + \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)}.]

In our expression, we have [MATH: n=-2] and [MATH: \varphi=\theta.] Substituting in these values, we get
[MATH: (1)/([\cos (θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (θ)]^{2})|= [\cos (θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (θ)]^{− 2}; = \cos (− 2θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (− 2θ).]

Finally, using the fact that [MATH: \cos(-\varphi) = \cos (\varphi)] and [MATH: \sin(-\varphi) = -\sin(\varphi)] for any input [MATH: \varphi,] we have
[MATH: \cos(-2\theta) + \textrm{i}\sin(-2\theta) = \cos(2\theta) - \textrm{i}\sin{(2\theta)}.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: De Moivre's Theorem With a Negative Sine

Content:
We can also use De Moivre's theorem for an expression with a subtraction:
[MATH: \left[ \cos (\varphi) - \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) - \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)}.]

Content:
For example, with [MATH: n=5] and [MATH: \varphi=3\theta,] we have

Content:
[MATH: [\cos (3θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (3θ)]^{5}|= \cos (5 ⋅ 3θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (5 ⋅ 3θ); = \cos (15θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (15θ).]

Content:
To understand why we can also use De Moivre's theorem with subtraction, remember that [MATH: \cos\varphi = \cos(-\varphi)] and [MATH: -\sin(\varphi) = \sin(-\varphi).] Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: [\cos (φ) − \textrm{i}\sin (φ)]^{n}|= [\cos (− φ) + \textrm{i}\sin (− φ)]^{n}; = \cos (− nφ) + \textrm{i}\sin (− nφ); = \cos (nφ) − \textrm{i}\sin (nφ).]

---

Explanation:

[MATH: (1)/([\cos (2θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (2θ)]^{4})|= [\cos (2θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (2θ)]^{− 4}.]

For expressions involving subtraction, De Moivre's theorem states that
[MATH: \left[ \cos (\varphi) - \textrm{i}\sin(\varphi) \right]^n = \cos(n\varphi) - \textrm{i}\sin{(n\varphi)}.]

In our expression, we have [MATH: n=-4] and [MATH: \varphi=2\theta.] Substituting in these values, we get
[MATH: [\cos (2θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (2θ)]^{− 4}|= \cos (− 4 ⋅ 2θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (− 4 ⋅ 2θ); = \cos (− 8θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (− 8θ).]

Finally, using the fact that [MATH: \cos(-\varphi) = \cos (\varphi)] and [MATH: \sin(-\varphi) = -\sin(\varphi)] for any input [MATH: \varphi,] we have
[MATH: \cos (− 8θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (− 8θ)|= \cos (8θ) − [− \textrm{i}\sin (8θ)]; = \cos (8θ) + \textrm{i}\sin (8θ).]
